tasks.title: Two Train Lines: A Cubic Velocity Model and a Distance Log
tasks.context: A transit authority studies the first two minutes of travel on two lines. On Line 1 the velocity of the train, in metres per second, is modelled for $0\le t\le 120$ by the polynomial $v(t)=0.00002t^{3}-0.005t^{2}+0.4t$, where $t$ is the time in seconds since departure. On Line 2 no formula is available; instead an odometer logged the distance travelled from the platform every ten seconds, as recorded in the table. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: At $t=80$ seconds the Line 1 train is decelerating.
The acceleration of the Line 1 train reaches its smallest value at some moment before $t=75$ seconds.
Over the whole two minutes the Line 2 train averaged more than $45$ km/h.
Among the ten-second stretches of the Line 2 log, exactly one interior stretch has a higher average velocity than both of its neighbours.
The highest ten-second average velocity on Line 2 is reached between $t=60$ and $t=70$ seconds.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Deceleration means the velocity is falling, and the rate at which velocity changes is the acceleration, obtained by differentiating the velocity model term by term. A negative acceleration is exactly a train slowing down.

$$v(t)=0.00002t^{3} - 0.005t^{2} + 0.4t$$

$$a(t)=0.00006t^{2} - 0.01t + 0.4$$

Substituting $t=80$:

$$a\left(80\right)=0.00006\cdot 80^{2} - 0.01\cdot 80 + 0.4=-0.016$$

The rate is $-0.016\ \text{m/s}^{2}$, which is negative, so $v$ is falling there, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The acceleration is the derivative of the velocity model, and that derivative is itself a quadratic in $t$. A quadratic with a positive leading coefficient opens upwards, so it has one lowest point and that point sits on its axis of symmetry.

$$v(t)=0.00002t^{3} - 0.005t^{2} + 0.4t$$

$$a(t)=0.00006t^{2} - 0.01t + 0.4$$

The leading coefficient $0.00006$ is positive, so the axis of symmetry carries the minimum.

$$t=-\frac{b}{2a}=\frac{0.01}{2\cdot 0.00006}=\frac{250}{3}$$

That is about $83.33$ seconds, and the acceleration there is the smallest value it takes on the whole interval.

$$a\left(\frac{250}{3}\right)=-\frac{1}{60}\approx -0.0167\ \text{m/s}^{2}$$

The smallest acceleration arrives after $75$ seconds, not before it, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

An average velocity is the total distance divided by the total time, so only the first and last rows of the log matter. The answer comes out in metres per second, and one metre per second is $3.6$ kilometres per hour.

$$\bar v=\frac{1400-0}{120-0}=\frac{35}{3}\approx 11.67\ \text{m/s}$$

Converting to the units used in the claim:

$$\frac{35}{3}\cdot 3.6=42\ \text{km/h}$$

The average is $42$ km/h, which does not clear the $45$ km/h mark, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Each row of the log gives a ten-second stretch, and the average velocity on a stretch is the distance gained there divided by ten seconds.

$$\bar v_{i}=\frac{d_{i+1}-d_{i}}{10}$$

Working through the twelve stretches in order gives, in metres per second,

$$7,\ 12,\ 14,\ 11,\ 15,\ 12,\ 13,\ 9,\ 14,\ 10,\ 11,\ 12$$

A stretch beats both neighbours whenever the sequence rises into it and falls out of it again, and that happens at the values $14,\ 15,\ 13,\ 14$.

There are four such stretches rather than a single one, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The stretch with the highest average velocity is the stretch on which the odometer gained the most metres, because every stretch lasts the same ten seconds.

$$\bar v_{60\text{–}70}=\frac{840-710}{10}=13\ \text{m/s}$$

The largest gain in the whole log is the one from $440$ to $590$ metres:

$$\bar v_{40\text{–}50}=\frac{590-440}{10}=15\ \text{m/s}$$

The record belongs to the $40$–$50$ second stretch at $15$ m/s, not to the $60$–$70$ stretch at $13$ m/s, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Line 1 is given by a cubic velocity model, so its acceleration is the quadratic obtained by differentiating it once.

$$v(t)=0.00002t^{3} - 0.005t^{2} + 0.4t$$

$$a(t)=0.00006t^{2} - 0.01t + 0.4$$

That quadratic opens upwards, so the acceleration bottoms out on its axis of symmetry and is negative around there — the train is losing speed.

$$t=\frac{250}{3}\approx 83.3\ \text{s}\qquad a(80)=-0.016$$

Line 2 has no formula, only a log, so every velocity question there is answered by dividing a distance gain by the ten seconds in which it happened.

$$\bar v=\frac{1400}{120}=\frac{35}{3}\ \text{m/s}=42\ \text{km/h}$$

The twelve stretch averages, in metres per second, are

$$7,\ 12,\ 14,\ 11,\ 15,\ 12,\ 13,\ 9,\ 14,\ 10,\ 11,\ 12$$

so the record stretch is $40$–$50$ seconds and the sequence peaks locally four separate times.

tasks.title: Reading Degree, Leading Coefficient and Constant Term
tasks.context: Consider the polynomial function $P(x)=2x^{4} - 5x^{3} + x - 7$, defined for every real $x$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The degree of $P$ is $4$.
The leading coefficient of $P$ is $-5$.
The graph of $P$ crosses the vertical axis at $\left(0,-7\right)$.
$P\left(1\right)=-9$.
As $x$ grows beyond every bound, $P\left(x\right)$ falls below every bound.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The degree is the largest power of the variable that still carries a non-zero coefficient, so order the terms by falling powers and look at the first one.

$$P(x)=2x^{4} - 5x^{3} + x - 7$$

The largest power present is $x^{4}$, and its coefficient $2$ is not zero.

$$\text{degree of }P=4$$

The degree is $4$, exactly the number in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The leading coefficient is the number sitting in front of the highest power, so order the terms by falling powers and read the first one.

$$P(x)=2x^{4} - 5x^{3} + x - 7$$

The highest power is $x^{4}$ and the number in front of it is what we are after.

$$\text{leading coefficient}=2$$

That number is $2$ while the claim says $-5$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The graph meets the vertical axis where the input is $0$, and at that input every term with a power of the variable disappears — only the constant term survives.

$$P(x)=2x^{4} - 5x^{3} + x - 7$$

$$P\left(0\right)=-7$$

The crossing sits at height $-7$, exactly where the claim puts it, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Evaluating a polynomial is substitution and nothing more: put the number in place of every occurrence of the variable and finish the arithmetic.

$$P(x)=2x^{4} - 5x^{3} + x - 7$$

Substituting $x=1$ term by term:

$$P\left(1\right)=2\cdot 1^{4} - 5\cdot 1^{3} + 1 - 7$$

$$P\left(1\right)=-9$$

The value is $-9$, exactly the figure in the claim, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Far away from the origin the highest power dwarfs everything else, so the far ends of the graph are decided by the leading term alone.

$$P(x)=2x^{4} - 5x^{3} + x - 7$$

$$\text{leading term}=2x^{4}$$

The exponent $4$ is even and the coefficient $2$ is positive, which fixes both ends of the picture.

On that side the values grow beyond every bound, the opposite of the claim, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything asked here is read off the polynomial once its terms are ordered by falling powers.

$$P(x)=2x^{4} - 5x^{3} + x - 7$$

The highest power is $x^{4}$, so the degree is $4$ and the leading coefficient is the $2$ in front of it. Setting $x=0$ kills every other term and leaves the constant.

$$\text{degree}=4\qquad \text{leading coefficient}=2\qquad P(0)=-7$$

Because the degree is even and the leading coefficient positive, both far ends of the graph climb.

tasks.title: Testing Candidate Zeros of a Cubic
tasks.context: A cubic function is given by $P(x)=x^{3} - 4x^{2} + x + 6$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $x=2$ is a zero of $P$.
$x=1$ is a zero of $P$.
$\left(x+1\right)$ is a factor of $P\left(x\right)$.
The graph of $P$ crosses the vertical axis at $\left(0,-6\right)$.
$P$ has exactly three distinct real zeros.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A zero is a number the function sends to $0$, so the check is a single substitution.

$$P(x)=x^{3} - 4x^{2} + x + 6$$

Putting $x=2$ into the expression:

$$P\left(2\right)=2^{3} - 4\cdot 2^{2} + 2 + 6=0$$

The function sends $2$ to $0$, which is what a zero means, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

A zero is a number the function sends to $0$, so the check is a single substitution.

$$P(x)=x^{3} - 4x^{2} + x + 6$$

Putting $x=1$ into the expression:

$$P\left(1\right)=1^{3} - 4\cdot 1^{2} + 1 + 6=4$$

The value there is $4$ and not $0$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

A linear bracket divides a polynomial exactly when the number that makes the bracket vanish is a zero of the polynomial, so there is nothing to divide: just substitute that number.

$$P(x)=x^{3} - 4x^{2} + x + 6$$

Putting $x=-1$ into the expression:

$$P\left(-1\right)=\left(-1\right)^{3} - 4\cdot \left(-1\right)^{2} + \left(-1\right) + 6=0$$

The substitution returns $0$, so the bracket divides $P$ with nothing left over, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

The graph meets the vertical axis where the input is $0$, and at that input every term with a power of the variable disappears — only the constant term survives.

$$P(x)=x^{3} - 4x^{2} + x + 6$$

$$P\left(0\right)=6$$

The crossing sits at height $6$, not at $-6$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Zeros are easiest to count from a factorised form, because a product is $0$ exactly when one of its factors is.

$$P(x)=x^{3} - 4x^{2} + x + 6$$

$$P\left(x\right)=\left(x+1\right)\left(x-2\right)\left(x-3\right)$$

Each bracket contributes the number that makes it vanish: $x=-1$, $x=2$, $x=3$.

There are three distinct real zeros, exactly the count claimed, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
A number is a zero of a polynomial exactly when substituting it returns $0$, and each zero corresponds to a linear factor.

$$P(x)=x^{3} - 4x^{2} + x + 6$$

$$P(x)=\left(x+1\right)\left(x-2\right)\left(x-3\right)$$

The three brackets vanish at $x=-1$, $x=2$ and $x=3$, so those are the zeros; any other candidate, $x=1$ included, must give a non-zero value.

$$P(-1)=0\qquad P(2)=0\qquad P(3)=0\qquad P(1)=4$$

tasks.title: Adding and Subtracting Two Cubics
tasks.context: Two polynomial functions are given by $f(x)=3x^{3} - x + 2$ and $g(x)=x^{3} + 4x^{2} - 5$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $f\left(x\right)+g\left(x\right)=4x^{3} + 4x^{2} - x - 3$.
The degree of $f\left(x\right)-g\left(x\right)$ is $3$.
In $f\left(x\right)+g\left(x\right)$ the constant term is $3$.
In $f\left(x\right)-g\left(x\right)$ the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is $4$.
The degree of $f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)$ is $6$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Adding two polynomials means adding the coefficients of matching powers, and nothing else happens.

$$f(x)=3x^{3} - x + 2\qquad g(x)=x^{3} + 4x^{2} - 5$$

$$f\left(x\right)+g\left(x\right)=4x^{3} + 4x^{2} - x - 3$$

The collected expression is exactly the one written in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Subtracting means changing every sign in the second function and then collecting matching powers.

$$f(x)=3x^{3} - x + 2\qquad g(x)=x^{3} + 4x^{2} - 5$$

$$f\left(x\right)-g\left(x\right)=2x^{3} - 4x^{2} - x + 7$$

The surviving highest power is $x^{3}$ with coefficient $2$.

The degree of the combination is $3$, the number claimed, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Adding two polynomials means adding the coefficients of matching powers, and nothing else happens.

$$f(x)=3x^{3} - x + 2\qquad g(x)=x^{3} + 4x^{2} - 5$$

$$f\left(x\right)+g\left(x\right)=4x^{3} + 4x^{2} - x - 3$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{0}=-3$$

That coefficient is $-3$ and the claim reports $3$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Subtracting means changing every sign in the second function and then collecting matching powers.

$$f(x)=3x^{3} - x + 2\qquad g(x)=x^{3} + 4x^{2} - 5$$

$$f\left(x\right)-g\left(x\right)=2x^{3} - 4x^{2} - x + 7$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{2}=-4$$

That coefficient is $-4$ and the claim reports $4$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Multiplying means every term of the first function meets every term of the second, after which matching powers are collected.

$$f(x)=3x^{3} - x + 2\qquad g(x)=x^{3} + 4x^{2} - 5$$

$$f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)=3x^{6} + 12x^{5} - x^{4} - 17x^{3} + 8x^{2} + 5x - 10$$

The surviving highest power is $x^{6}$ with coefficient $3$.

The degree of the combination is $6$, the number claimed, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Sums and differences of polynomials are settled power by power; products raise the degree by adding the two degrees.

$$f(x)=3x^{3} - x + 2\qquad g(x)=x^{3} + 4x^{2} - 5$$

$$f(x)+g(x)=4x^{3} + 4x^{2} - x - 3$$

$$f(x)-g(x)=2x^{3} - 4x^{2} - x + 7$$

Both functions have degree $3$, so their product has degree $6$ while the sum and the difference stay at degree $3$ — the leading terms $3x^{3}$ and $x^{3}$ do not cancel.

tasks.title: Reading a Cubic Off Its Graph
tasks.context: The figure shows the graph of a polynomial function $f$ over the window $-2\le x\le 4$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The graph of $f$ crosses the vertical axis at $\left(0,3\right)$.
The curve meets the horizontal axis exactly three times.
The graph of $f$ has exactly one turning point.
At $x=0$ the graph of $f$ lies below the horizontal axis.
As $x$ grows beyond every bound, $f\left(x\right)$ grows beyond every bound.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The graph meets the vertical axis where the input is $0$, and at that input every term with a power of the variable disappears — only the constant term survives.

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x^{2} - x + 3$$

$$f\left(0\right)=3$$

The crossing sits at height $3$, exactly where the claim puts it, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Crossings of the horizontal axis are the zeros of the function, and a factorised form shows them all at once.

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x^{2} - x + 3$$

$$f\left(x\right)=\left(x+1\right)\left(x-1\right)\left(x-3\right)$$

Each bracket contributes the number that makes it vanish: $x=-1$, $x=1$, $x=3$.

There are three distinct real zeros, exactly the count claimed, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A turning point is a place where the curve stops rising and starts falling, or the other way round; a polynomial of degree $n$ can have at most $n-1$ of them.

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x^{2} - x + 3$$

The picture changes direction at $x\approx -0.15$, $x\approx 2.15$, and between those places the curve keeps one direction throughout.

$$\text{turning points of }f=2$$

There are two turning points while the claim insists on one, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Whether the curve runs under or over the horizontal axis at a given input is decided by the sign of the value there, so evaluate and look at the sign.

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x^{2} - x + 3$$

$$f\left(0\right)=0^{3} - 3\cdot 0^{2} - 0 + 3=3$$

The value $3$ is positive, so the curve runs above the axis there, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Far away from the origin the highest power dwarfs everything else, so the far ends of the graph are decided by the leading term alone.

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x^{2} - x + 3$$

$$\text{leading term}=x^{3}$$

The exponent $3$ is odd and the coefficient $1$ is positive, which fixes both ends of the picture.

On that side the values grow beyond every bound, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The picture belongs to the cubic

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x^{2} - x + 3$$

$$f(x)=\left(x+1\right)\left(x-1\right)\left(x-3\right)$$

so the curve cuts the horizontal axis at $x=-1$, $x=1$ and $x=3$ and meets the vertical axis at height $3$.

$$f(0)=3$$

Between the outer crossings the curve turns twice, once up and once down, and because the leading coefficient is positive the right-hand arm climbs without bound.

tasks.title: A Cubic Cost Curve for a Small Workshop
tasks.context: A workshop's weekly production cost, in hundreds of euros, is modelled by $C(q)=q^{3} - 12q^{2} + 60q + 200$, where $q$ is the number of batches produced per week and $0\le q\le 10$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Producing nothing at all still costs $200$ hundred euros.
$C\left(2\right)=280$ hundred euros.
$C\left(5\right)=335$ hundred euros.
The degree of $C$ is $2$.
Between $q=0$ and $q=5$ the cost grows on average by $25$ hundred euros per batch.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Fixed cost is what the model charges when output is zero, and putting $q=0$ into a polynomial leaves only its constant term.

$$C(q)=q^{3} - 12q^{2} + 60q + 200$$

Substituting $q=0$ term by term:

$$C\left(0\right)=0^{3} - 12\cdot 0^{2} + 60\cdot 0 + 200$$

$$C\left(0\right)=200$$

The value is $200$ hundred euros, exactly the figure in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Evaluating a polynomial is substitution and nothing more: put the number in place of every occurrence of the variable and finish the arithmetic.

$$C(q)=q^{3} - 12q^{2} + 60q + 200$$

Substituting $q=2$ term by term:

$$C\left(2\right)=2^{3} - 12\cdot 2^{2} + 60\cdot 2 + 200$$

$$C\left(2\right)=280$$

The value is $280$ hundred euros, exactly the figure in the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Evaluating a polynomial is substitution and nothing more: put the number in place of every occurrence of the variable and finish the arithmetic.

$$C(q)=q^{3} - 12q^{2} + 60q + 200$$

Substituting $q=5$ term by term:

$$C\left(5\right)=5^{3} - 12\cdot 5^{2} + 60\cdot 5 + 200$$

$$C\left(5\right)=325$$

The value is $325$ hundred euros while the claim reports $335$ hundred euros, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The degree is the largest power of the variable that still carries a non-zero coefficient, so order the terms by falling powers and look at the first one.

$$C(q)=q^{3} - 12q^{2} + 60q + 200$$

The largest power present is $q^{3}$, and its coefficient $1$ is not zero.

$$\text{degree of }C=3$$

The degree is $3$ and the claim names $2$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

An average rate of change is the total change in the output divided by the change in the input, so both endpoint values are needed first.

$$C(q)=q^{3} - 12q^{2} + 60q + 200$$

$$C\left(0\right)=200\qquad C\left(5\right)=325$$

Dividing the change in the output by the change in the input:

$$\frac{325-\left(200\right)}{5-\left(0\right)}=25$$

The average rate is $25$ hundred euros per batch, which is what the claim asks for, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The model is a cubic in the number of batches, so every question is answered by substitution.

$$C(q)=q^{3} - 12q^{2} + 60q + 200$$

$$C(0)=200\qquad C(2)=280\qquad C(5)=325$$

The highest power is $q^{3}$, so the degree is $3$, and an average growth rate is a change in cost divided by the change in output.

$$\frac{C(5)-C(0)}{5-0}=\frac{125}{5}=25$$

tasks.title: Cumulative Output Recorded Hour by Hour
tasks.context: A bottling line logs the number of crates completed since the start of the shift, measured at the end of each hour. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The hour-by-hour gains recorded in the table are not all equal.
Differencing the table twice produces a constant row.
The line completed $36$ crates during the fifth hour.
Because the second differences are constant, a linear model in $h$ fits the cumulative totals exactly.
Over the whole five hours the line averaged $28$ crates per hour.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

For inputs spaced equally apart, differencing a table repeatedly strips one degree away each time, so a polynomial of degree $k$ flattens out to a constant exactly at the $k$-th round of differences.

$$\text{first differences}: 12,\ 20,\ 28,\ 36,\ 44$$

The first row still moves, so the flattening has not happened yet.

The first differences of the cumulative crate counts are not constant, which is what the claim describes, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

For inputs spaced equally apart, differencing a table repeatedly strips one degree away each time, so a polynomial of degree $k$ flattens out to a constant exactly at the $k$-th round of differences.

$$\text{first differences}: 12,\ 20,\ 28,\ 36,\ 44$$

$$\text{second differences}: 8,\ 8,\ 8,\ 8$$

The second row repeats the single value $8$ all the way across.

The second differences of the cumulative crate counts are constant, which is what the claim describes, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A single hour's output is the difference between two consecutive cumulative readings, because the table records running totals rather than hourly figures. The fifth hour runs from the reading at $h=4$ to the reading at $h=5$.

$$140-96=44$$

The figure $36$ does appear among the hourly gains, but one row earlier:

$$96-60=36$$

The fifth hour added $44$ crates and the $36$ belongs to the fourth hour, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Differencing a table of equally spaced readings strips one degree away each round, so the row that first becomes constant tells us the degree of the polynomial behind the data.

$$\text{first differences}: 12,\ 20,\ 28,\ 36,\ 44$$

$$\text{second differences}: 8,\ 8,\ 8,\ 8$$

A linear model would already have constant first differences, and these are still climbing by $8$ each time; the row that flattens is the second, which points to degree $2$.

The data need a quadratic in $h$, so a linear model cannot fit them exactly, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

An average per hour is the total produced divided by the number of hours, so only the first and last rows are needed.

$$\frac{140-0}{5-0}=28$$

The shift averaged $28$ crates an hour as claimed, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The readings are one hour apart, so differencing them is the natural first move.

$$\text{totals}: 0,\ 12,\ 32,\ 60,\ 96,\ 140$$

$$\text{first differences}: 12,\ 20,\ 28,\ 36,\ 44$$

$$\text{second differences}: 8,\ 8,\ 8,\ 8$$

The second row is constant, so the cumulative totals follow a quadratic in $h$ — not a linear one — and each single hour's output is one first difference.

tasks.title: Multiplying Two Linear Functions
tasks.context: Two linear functions are given by $f(x)=2x - 3$ and $g(x)=x + 5$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)=2x^{2} + 7x - 15$.
The degree of $f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)$ is $2$.
In $f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)$ the constant term is $-13$.
The degree of $f\left(x\right)+g\left(x\right)$ is $2$.
The product $f(x)g(x)$ has exactly two distinct real zeros.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Multiplying means every term of the first function meets every term of the second, after which matching powers are collected.

$$f(x)=2x - 3\qquad g(x)=x + 5$$

$$f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)=2x^{2} + 7x - 15$$

The collected expression is exactly the one written in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Multiplying means every term of the first function meets every term of the second, after which matching powers are collected.

$$f(x)=2x - 3\qquad g(x)=x + 5$$

$$f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)=2x^{2} + 7x - 15$$

The surviving highest power is $x^{2}$ with coefficient $2$.

The degree of the combination is $2$, the number claimed, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Multiplying means every term of the first function meets every term of the second, after which matching powers are collected.

$$f(x)=2x - 3\qquad g(x)=x + 5$$

$$f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)=2x^{2} + 7x - 15$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{0}=-15$$

That coefficient is $-15$ and the claim reports $-13$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Adding two polynomials means adding the coefficients of matching powers, and nothing else happens.

$$f(x)=2x - 3\qquad g(x)=x + 5$$

$$f\left(x\right)+g\left(x\right)=3x + 2$$

The surviving highest power is $x^{1}$ with coefficient $3$.

The degree of the combination is $1$ while the claim says $2$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

Zeros are easiest to count from a factorised form, because a product is $0$ exactly when one of its factors is.

$$fg(x)=2x^{2} + 7x - 15$$

$$fg\left(x\right)=2\left(x-\frac{3}{2}\right)\left(x+5\right)$$

Each bracket contributes the number that makes it vanish: $x=\frac{3}{2}$, $x=-5$.

There are two distinct real zeros, exactly the count claimed, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Each term of the first bracket meets each term of the second, and matching powers are then collected.

$$f(x)=2x - 3\qquad g(x)=x + 5$$

$$f(x)g(x)=2x^{2} + 7x - 15$$

Degrees add under multiplication, $1+1=2$, but a sum of two linear functions is still linear.

$$f(x)+g(x)=3x + 2$$

A product is zero when a factor is, so the zeros are $x=\frac{3}{2}$ and $x=-5$.

tasks.title: Degrees of Sums and Products Without Numbers
tasks.context: Let $f$ and $g$ be polynomial functions of degree $3$ and degree $2$ respectively, with no further information about their coefficients. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The product $f\cdot g$ always has degree $5$.
The sum $f+g$ always has degree $3$.
The difference $f-g$ can have degree $2$ for a suitable choice of $f$ and $g$.
The function $f\cdot f$ always has degree $6$.
The constant term of $f\cdot g$ is always zero.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

When two polynomials are multiplied, the highest power of the answer comes from the two leading terms meeting each other, and no other pairing can reach that high.

$$a x^{3}\cdot b x^{2}=ab\,x^{5}$$

Leading coefficients are non-zero by definition, so the product $ab$ is non-zero too and the $x^{5}$ term genuinely survives.

The degrees add, $3+2=5$, in every case, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Adding polynomials adds coefficients of matching powers, so a term can only disappear if the other function has a term of the same power to cancel it.

$$f(x)+g(x)=a x^{3}+\left(\text{powers no higher than }x^{2}\right)$$

The function $g$ has degree $2$, so it contributes nothing at the level of $x^{3}$ and the leading term of $f$ survives untouched.

The sum keeps the degree $3$ of the larger of the two, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Subtracting changes every sign in $g$ and then collects matching powers, so the $x^{3}$ term of $f$ again meets nothing to cancel it.

$$f(x)-g(x)=a x^{3}+\left(\text{powers no higher than }x^{2}\right)$$

With $a\neq 0$ the cubic term is still there whatever $g$ does at the lower powers.

The difference always has degree $3$, so degree $2$ is out of reach, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Squaring is multiplying a polynomial by itself, so the same rule about leading terms applies.

$$a x^{3}\cdot a x^{3}=a^{2}x^{6}$$

Since $a\neq 0$, the square $a^{2}$ is non-zero as well.

The degree doubles from $3$ to $6$ every time, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

The constant term of a product is the product of the two constant terms, since that is the only way to end up with no factor of $x$ at all.

$$f(0)\cdot g(0)$$

Nothing in the statement forces either constant term to vanish; a single example settles it.

$$\left(x^{3}+1\right)\left(x^{2}+1\right)=x^{5}+x^{3}+x^{2}+1$$

That product ends in a constant term of $1$, not $0$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Only two structural rules are in play, and both concern the leading terms.

$$\text{degree}(fg)=\text{degree}(f)+\text{degree}(g)$$

$$\text{degree}(f\pm g)=\max\left(3,2\right)=3$$

Degrees add under multiplication because the two leading terms meet; under addition the larger degree survives whenever the two degrees differ, because there is nothing at that level to cancel against.

tasks.title: Two Curves, One Picture: Which Arm Goes Where
tasks.context: The figure shows two polynomial graphs on the same axes: the solid curve is $y=f(x)$ and the dashed curve is $y=g(x)$, drawn for $-3\le x\le 3$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: As $x$ grows beyond every bound, $f\left(x\right)$ falls below every bound.
As $x$ grows beyond every bound, $g\left(x\right)$ falls below every bound.
The graph of $f$ crosses the vertical axis at $\left(0,0\right)$.
The graph of $f$ has exactly three turning points.
Both curves pass through the origin.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Far away from the origin the highest power dwarfs everything else, so the far ends of the graph are decided by the leading term alone.

$$f(x)=-x^{3} + 4x$$

$$\text{leading term}=-x^{3}$$

The exponent $3$ is odd and the coefficient $-1$ is negative, which fixes both ends of the picture.

On that side the values fall below every bound, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Far away from the origin the highest power dwarfs everything else, so the far ends of the graph are decided by the leading term alone.

$$g(x)=x^{3} - 3x$$

$$\text{leading term}=x^{3}$$

The exponent $3$ is odd and the coefficient $1$ is positive, which fixes both ends of the picture.

On that side the values grow beyond every bound, the opposite of the claim, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The graph meets the vertical axis where the input is $0$, and at that input every term with a power of the variable disappears — only the constant term survives.

$$f(x)=-x^{3} + 4x$$

$$f\left(0\right)=0$$

The crossing sits at height $0$, exactly where the claim puts it, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A turning point is a place where the curve stops rising and starts falling, or the other way round; a polynomial of degree $n$ can have at most $n-1$ of them.

$$f(x)=-x^{3} + 4x$$

The picture changes direction at $x\approx -1.15$, $x\approx 1.15$, and between those places the curve keeps one direction throughout.

$$\text{turning points of }f=2$$

There are two turning points while the claim insists on three, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

A curve runs through the origin exactly when its value at $x=0$ is $0$, and at that input only the constant term of a polynomial survives.

$$f(x)=-x^{3} + 4x$$

$$g(x)=x^{3} - 3x$$

Neither expression carries a constant term, so both vanish at $x=0$.

$$f(0)=0\qquad g(0)=0$$

Both graphs go through $(0,0)$ as the picture suggests, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The two functions in the picture are

$$f(x)=-x^{3} + 4x$$

$$g(x)=x^{3} - 3x$$

Both are odd cubics through the origin, but their leading coefficients have opposite signs, so their right-hand arms head in opposite directions: $f$ dives, $g$ climbs. Each has two turning points.

tasks.title: A Quadratic Temperature Model Through the Morning
tasks.context: In a greenhouse the temperature in degrees Celsius above the outside air is modelled by $T(d)=-d^{2} + 6d + 4$, where $d$ is the number of hours since sunrise and $0\le d\le 7$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $T\left(0\right)=4$ degrees.
$T\left(3\right)=13$ degrees.
$T\left(6\right)=6$ degrees.
The degree of $T$ is $3$.
Across the first three hours the model warms by $3$ degrees per hour on average.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Evaluating a polynomial is substitution and nothing more: put the number in place of every occurrence of the variable and finish the arithmetic.

$$T(d)=-d^{2} + 6d + 4$$

Substituting $d=0$ term by term:

$$T\left(0\right)=-0^{2} + 6\cdot 0 + 4$$

$$T\left(0\right)=4$$

The value is $4$ degrees, exactly the figure in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Evaluating a polynomial is substitution and nothing more: put the number in place of every occurrence of the variable and finish the arithmetic.

$$T(d)=-d^{2} + 6d + 4$$

Substituting $d=3$ term by term:

$$T\left(3\right)=-3^{2} + 6\cdot 3 + 4$$

$$T\left(3\right)=13$$

The value is $13$ degrees, exactly the figure in the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Evaluating a polynomial is substitution and nothing more: put the number in place of every occurrence of the variable and finish the arithmetic.

$$T(d)=-d^{2} + 6d + 4$$

Substituting $d=6$ term by term:

$$T\left(6\right)=-6^{2} + 6\cdot 6 + 4$$

$$T\left(6\right)=4$$

The value is $4$ degrees while the claim reports $6$ degrees, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

The degree is the largest power of the variable that still carries a non-zero coefficient, so order the terms by falling powers and look at the first one.

$$T(d)=-d^{2} + 6d + 4$$

The largest power present is $d^{2}$, and its coefficient $-1$ is not zero.

$$\text{degree of }T=2$$

The degree is $2$ and the claim names $3$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

An average rate of change is the total change in the output divided by the change in the input, so both endpoint values are needed first.

$$T(d)=-d^{2} + 6d + 4$$

$$T\left(0\right)=4\qquad T\left(3\right)=13$$

Dividing the change in the output by the change in the input:

$$\frac{13-\left(4\right)}{3-\left(0\right)}=3$$

The average rate is $3$ degrees per hour, which is what the claim asks for, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The model is a quadratic in the number of hours since sunrise.

$$T(d)=-d^{2} + 6d + 4$$

$$T(0)=4\qquad T(3)=13\qquad T(6)=4$$

The leading coefficient $-1$ is negative, so the curve opens downwards and the warmest moment is its turning point at $d=3$; the model is symmetric about that hour, which is why $d=0$ and $d=6$ give the same reading.

$$\frac{T(3)-T(0)}{3-0}=\frac{9}{3}=3$$

tasks.title: Factor Theorem and Remainders on a Cubic
tasks.context: Let $P(x)=2x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 11x + 6$ for every real $x$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $\left(x-3\right)$ is a factor of $P\left(x\right)$.
Dividing $P\left(x\right)$ by $\left(x-1\right)$ leaves the remainder $6$.
$x=-\frac{1}{2}$ is a zero of $P$.
$P$ has exactly three distinct real zeros.
$P\left(2\right)=-12$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A linear bracket divides a polynomial exactly when the number that makes the bracket vanish is a zero of the polynomial, so there is nothing to divide: just substitute that number.

$$P(x)=2x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 11x + 6$$

Putting $x=3$ into the expression:

$$P\left(3\right)=2\cdot 3^{3} - 3\cdot 3^{2} - 11\cdot 3 + 6=0$$

The substitution returns $0$, so the bracket divides $P$ with nothing left over, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Dividing by a linear bracket leaves a constant remainder, and that constant is just the value of the polynomial at the number which kills the bracket.

$$P(x)=2x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 11x + 6$$

The bracket vanishes at $x=1$, so evaluate there:

$$P\left(1\right)=2\cdot 1^{3} - 3\cdot 1^{2} - 11\cdot 1 + 6=-6$$

The quotient is $2x^{2} - x - 12$, and the division reads

$$2x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 11x + 6=\left(x-1\right)\left(2x^{2} - x - 12\right)-6$$

The remainder is $-6$ while the claim announces $6$, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

A zero is a number the function sends to $0$, so the check is a single substitution.

$$P(x)=2x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 11x + 6$$

Putting $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ into the expression:

$$P\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=2\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{3} - 3\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} - 11\cdot \left(-\frac{1}{2}\right) + 6=\frac{21}{2}$$

The value there is $\frac{21}{2}$ and not $0$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Zeros are easiest to count from a factorised form, because a product is $0$ exactly when one of its factors is.

$$P(x)=2x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 11x + 6$$

$$P\left(x\right)=2\left(x+2\right)\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(x-3\right)$$

Each bracket contributes the number that makes it vanish: $x=-2$, $x=\frac{1}{2}$, $x=3$.

There are three distinct real zeros, exactly the count claimed, so the statement is True.

**E.** → True

Evaluating a polynomial is substitution and nothing more: put the number in place of every occurrence of the variable and finish the arithmetic.

$$P(x)=2x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 11x + 6$$

Substituting $x=2$ term by term:

$$P\left(2\right)=2\cdot 2^{3} - 3\cdot 2^{2} - 11\cdot 2 + 6$$

$$P\left(2\right)=-12$$

The value is $-12$, exactly the figure in the claim, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Everything here rests on one fact: substituting a number into a polynomial gives the remainder left by dividing out the matching linear bracket, so a zero and a factor are the same piece of information.

$$P(x)=2x^{3} - 3x^{2} - 11x + 6$$

$$P(x)=2\left(x+2\right)\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)\left(x-3\right)$$

The three brackets vanish at $x=-2$, $x=\frac{1}{2}$ and $x=3$, so those are the zeros; any other input leaves a non-zero remainder.

$$P(1)=-6\qquad P(2)=-12\qquad P\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{21}{2}$$

tasks.title: Hunting Coefficients in a Product
tasks.context: Two functions are given by $f(x)=x - 4$ and $g(x)=3x^{2} + x - 2$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)=3x^{3} - 11x^{2} - 6x + 8$.
In $f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)$ the coefficient of $x^{2}$ is $-11$.
In $f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)$ the constant term is $-8$.
The degree of $f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)$ is $3$.
The degree of $f\left(x\right)+g\left(x\right)$ is $3$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Multiplying means every term of the first function meets every term of the second, after which matching powers are collected.

$$f(x)=x - 4\qquad g(x)=3x^{2} + x - 2$$

$$f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)=3x^{3} - 11x^{2} - 6x + 8$$

The collected expression is exactly the one written in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Multiplying means every term of the first function meets every term of the second, after which matching powers are collected.

$$f(x)=x - 4\qquad g(x)=3x^{2} + x - 2$$

$$f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)=3x^{3} - 11x^{2} - 6x + 8$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{2}=-11$$

That coefficient is $-11$, exactly the value claimed, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Multiplying means every term of the first function meets every term of the second, after which matching powers are collected.

$$f(x)=x - 4\qquad g(x)=3x^{2} + x - 2$$

$$f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)=3x^{3} - 11x^{2} - 6x + 8$$

$$\text{coefficient of }x^{0}=8$$

That coefficient is $8$ and the claim reports $-8$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Multiplying means every term of the first function meets every term of the second, after which matching powers are collected.

$$f(x)=x - 4\qquad g(x)=3x^{2} + x - 2$$

$$f\left(x\right)\cdot g\left(x\right)=3x^{3} - 11x^{2} - 6x + 8$$

The surviving highest power is $x^{3}$ with coefficient $3$.

The degree of the combination is $3$, the number claimed, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Adding two polynomials means adding the coefficients of matching powers, and nothing else happens.

$$f(x)=x - 4\qquad g(x)=3x^{2} + x - 2$$

$$f\left(x\right)+g\left(x\right)=3x^{2} + 2x - 6$$

The surviving highest power is $x^{2}$ with coefficient $3$.

The degree of the combination is $2$ while the claim says $3$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Multiplying a linear function by a quadratic one gives every term of the first a turn against every term of the second.

$$f(x)=x - 4\qquad g(x)=3x^{2} + x - 2$$

$$f(x)g(x)=3x^{3} - 11x^{2} - 6x + 8$$

Degrees add here, $1+2=3$, but adding the two functions cannot lift anything above the quadratic already present in $g$.

$$f(x)+g(x)=3x^{2} + 2x - 6$$

tasks.title: Both Arms of a Quartic With a Negative Lead
tasks.context: Consider the polynomial function $P(x)=-2x^{4} + x^{3} - 5$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The degree of $P$ is $4$.
The leading coefficient of $P$ is $-2$.
As $x$ grows beyond every bound, $P\left(x\right)$ falls below every bound.
As $x$ falls below every bound, $P\left(x\right)$ grows beyond every bound.
The graph of $P$ crosses the vertical axis at $\left(0,5\right)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The degree is the largest power of the variable that still carries a non-zero coefficient, so order the terms by falling powers and look at the first one.

$$P(x)=-2x^{4} + x^{3} - 5$$

The largest power present is $x^{4}$, and its coefficient $-2$ is not zero.

$$\text{degree of }P=4$$

The degree is $4$, exactly the number in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The leading coefficient is the number sitting in front of the highest power, so order the terms by falling powers and read the first one.

$$P(x)=-2x^{4} + x^{3} - 5$$

The highest power is $x^{4}$ and the number in front of it is what we are after.

$$\text{leading coefficient}=-2$$

That number is $-2$, exactly what the claim says, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Far away from the origin the highest power dwarfs everything else, so the far ends of the graph are decided by the leading term alone.

$$P(x)=-2x^{4} + x^{3} - 5$$

$$\text{leading term}=-2x^{4}$$

The exponent $4$ is even and the coefficient $-2$ is negative, which fixes both ends of the picture.

On that side the values fall below every bound, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Far away from the origin the highest power dwarfs everything else, so the far ends of the graph are decided by the leading term alone.

$$P(x)=-2x^{4} + x^{3} - 5$$

$$\text{leading term}=-2x^{4}$$

The exponent $4$ is even and the coefficient $-2$ is negative, which fixes both ends of the picture.

On that side the values fall below every bound, the opposite of the claim, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The graph meets the vertical axis where the input is $0$, and at that input every term with a power of the variable disappears — only the constant term survives.

$$P(x)=-2x^{4} + x^{3} - 5$$

$$P\left(0\right)=-5$$

The crossing sits at height $-5$, not at $5$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
For large inputs the quartic term decides everything, so both arms of the graph follow the sign of $-2x^{4}$.

$$P(x)=-2x^{4} + x^{3} - 5$$

$$\text{leading term}=-2x^{4}$$

An even power keeps the sign of $x^{4}$ positive on both sides, and the factor $-2$ then turns both arms downwards. Only the constant term survives at $x=0$.

$$P(0)=-5$$

tasks.title: A Quartic Graph With Four Crossings
tasks.context: The figure shows the graph of a polynomial function $f$ on the window $-2.6\le x\le 2.6$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The curve meets the horizontal axis exactly four times.
The graph of $f$ crosses the vertical axis at $\left(0,4\right)$.
The graph of $f$ has exactly two turning points.
The curve is symmetric about the vertical axis.
As $x$ falls below every bound, $f\left(x\right)$ falls below every bound.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

The crossings are the zeros of the function, and here the expression splits into linear brackets, each handing over one crossing.

$$f(x)=x^{4} - 5x^{2} + 4$$

$$f\left(x\right)=\left(x+2\right)\left(x+1\right)\left(x-1\right)\left(x-2\right)$$

Each bracket contributes the number that makes it vanish: $x=-2$, $x=-1$, $x=1$, $x=2$.

There are four distinct real zeros, exactly the count claimed, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The graph meets the vertical axis where the input is $0$, and at that input every term with a power of the variable disappears — only the constant term survives.

$$f(x)=x^{4} - 5x^{2} + 4$$

$$f\left(0\right)=4$$

The crossing sits at height $4$, exactly where the claim puts it, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A turning point is a place where the curve stops rising and starts falling, or the other way round; a polynomial of degree $n$ can have at most $n-1$ of them.

$$f(x)=x^{4} - 5x^{2} + 4$$

The picture changes direction at $x\approx -1.58$, $x\approx 0$, $x\approx 1.58$, and between those places the curve keeps one direction throughout.

$$\text{turning points of }f=3$$

There are three turning points while the claim insists on two, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

A graph is symmetric about the vertical axis exactly when replacing $x$ by $-x$ leaves the function unchanged, and that happens when only even powers appear.

$$f(x)=x^{4} - 5x^{2} + 4$$

Every power present here is even, and an even power cannot notice a change of sign in the input.

$$f(-x)=\left(-x\right)^{4}-5\left(-x\right)^{2}+4=x^{4}-5x^{2}+4$$

The two expressions agree for every $x$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Far away from the origin the highest power dwarfs everything else, so the far ends of the graph are decided by the leading term alone.

$$f(x)=x^{4} - 5x^{2} + 4$$

$$\text{leading term}=x^{4}$$

The exponent $4$ is even and the coefficient $1$ is positive, which fixes both ends of the picture.

On that side the values grow beyond every bound, the opposite of the claim, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The curve in the picture belongs to

$$f(x)=x^{4} - 5x^{2} + 4$$

$$f(x)=\left(x+2\right)\left(x+1\right)\left(x-1\right)\left(x-2\right)$$

so it cuts the horizontal axis at $x=-2,-1,1,2$ and passes the vertical axis at height $4$. Only even powers appear, which is the symmetry visible in the drawing.

$$f(0)=4$$

Between the four crossings the curve must turn three times, and both arms climb because the degree is even with a positive leading coefficient.

tasks.title: Where a Cubic Only Touches the Axis
tasks.context: The figure shows the graph of a polynomial function $f$ on the window $-3\le x\le 2.5$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The curve meets the horizontal axis at exactly two places.
$x=1$ is a zero of $f$.
At $x=1$ the curve passes from one side of the horizontal axis to the other.
The graph of $f$ crosses the vertical axis at $\left(0,2\right)$.
The graph of $f$ has exactly three turning points.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Two of the three linear factors of this cubic turn out to be the same, so the list of crossings is shorter than the degree.

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x + 2$$

$$f\left(x\right)=\left(x+2\right)\left(x-1\right)$$

Each bracket contributes the number that makes it vanish: $x=-2$, $x=1$.

There are two distinct real zeros, exactly the count claimed, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

A zero is a number the function sends to $0$, so the check is a single substitution.

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x + 2$$

Putting $x=1$ into the expression:

$$f\left(1\right)=1^{3} - 3\cdot 1 + 2=0$$

The function sends $1$ to $0$, which is what a zero means, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

A curve changes side only if the values around the zero have opposite signs, so the sign just left and just right of $x=1$ decides it.

$$f(x)=\left(x-1\right)^{2}\left(x+2\right)$$

The bracket $\left(x-1\right)^{2}$ is a square, so it is never negative, and near $x=1$ the other bracket $\left(x+2\right)$ stays positive.

$$f(0.9)=0.029\qquad f(1.1)=0.031$$

The values on both sides are positive, so the curve only touches the axis and turns back, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The graph meets the vertical axis where the input is $0$, and at that input every term with a power of the variable disappears — only the constant term survives.

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x + 2$$

$$f\left(0\right)=2$$

The crossing sits at height $2$, exactly where the claim puts it, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

A turning point is a place where the curve stops rising and starts falling, or the other way round; a polynomial of degree $n$ can have at most $n-1$ of them.

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x + 2$$

The picture changes direction at $x\approx -1$, $x\approx 1$, and between those places the curve keeps one direction throughout.

$$\text{turning points of }f=2$$

There are two turning points while the claim insists on three, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The picture belongs to the cubic

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x + 2$$

$$f(x)=\left(x-1\right)^{2}\left(x+2\right)$$

The repeated bracket at $x=1$ is a square, so the curve reaches the axis there and bounces back instead of crossing; at $x=-2$ the single bracket lets it pass through.

$$f(0)=2\qquad f(1)=0\qquad f(-2)=0$$

There are two turning points: the local maximum at $x=-1$ and the touching point at $x=1$ itself.

tasks.title: An Open Box Cut From a Rectangular Sheet
tasks.context: A square of side $x$ centimetres is cut from each corner of a $20$ cm by $12$ cm metal sheet, and the flaps are folded up to form an open box. The volume in cubic centimetres is therefore $V(x)=x\left(20-2x\right)\left(12-2x\right)$, with $0<x<6$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Expanding the three brackets gives $V(x)=4x^{3} - 64x^{2} + 240x$.
Cutting corners of side $2$ cm gives a box of volume $256$ cm$^{3}$.
At $x=6$ the formula returns a volume of zero.
Cutting corners of side $3$ cm gives a larger box than cutting $2$ cm.
The degree of $V$ is $2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Multiplying out is a matter of taking the two large brackets first and then letting the factor $x$ through.

$$\left(20-2x\right)\left(12-2x\right)=240-64x+4x^{2}$$

Multiplying that by the remaining factor $x$ raises every power by one:

$$V(x)=4x^{3} - 64x^{2} + 240x$$

The expansion matches the cubic written in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Evaluating a polynomial is substitution and nothing more: put the number in place of every occurrence of the variable and finish the arithmetic.

$$V(x)=4x^{3} - 64x^{2} + 240x$$

Substituting $x=2$ term by term:

$$V\left(2\right)=4\cdot 2^{3} - 64\cdot 2^{2} + 240\cdot 2$$

$$V\left(2\right)=256$$

The value is $256$ cubic centimetres, exactly the figure in the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The formula is a product, so it vanishes as soon as one of its factors does; the geometry says the same thing, because a $12$ cm side loses two flaps of $6$ cm and nothing is left to fold.

$$V(6)=6\left(20-12\right)\left(12-12\right)$$

$$V(6)=0$$

The middle bracket closes at $x=6$ and the volume collapses to $0$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

Comparing two boxes needs nothing but the two volumes, and each of them is one substitution into the expanded cubic.

$$V(2)=4\cdot 2^{3} - 64\cdot 2^{2} + 240\cdot 2=256$$

$$V(3)=4\cdot 3^{3} - 64\cdot 3^{2} + 240\cdot 3=252$$

The $3$ cm corner takes more metal out of the base than it adds in height, so the box comes out slightly smaller.

At $252$ against $256$ cubic centimetres the $3$ cm box loses, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The degree is the largest power of the variable that still carries a non-zero coefficient, so order the terms by falling powers and look at the first one.

$$V(x)=4x^{3} - 64x^{2} + 240x$$

The largest power present is $x^{3}$, and its coefficient $4$ is not zero.

$$\text{degree of }V=3$$

The degree is $3$ and the claim names $2$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The three brackets multiply out to a cubic in the corner size.

$$V(x)=4x^{3} - 64x^{2} + 240x$$

$$V(2)=256\qquad V(3)=252\qquad V(6)=0$$

So a $2$ cm corner already beats a $3$ cm corner, and at $x=6$ the box has no base left at all. The highest power is $x^{3}$, so the model has degree $3$.

tasks.title: Morning Water Demand as a Cubic
tasks.context: A utility models the town's water draw, in thousands of litres per hour, by $D(t)=0.5t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 18t + 40$, where $t$ is the number of hours after 6 a.m. and $0\le t\le 8$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $D\left(2\right)=56$ thousand litres per hour.
$D\left(4\right)=52$ thousand litres per hour.
Between 6 a.m. and 10 a.m. the draw grows on average by $2$ thousand litres per hour, for each hour that passes.
The draw at noon is the same as the draw at 6 a.m.
At 10 a.m. the draw is still rising.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Evaluating a polynomial is substitution and nothing more: put the number in place of every occurrence of the variable and finish the arithmetic.

$$D(t)=0.5t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 18t + 40$$

Substituting $t=2$ term by term:

$$D\left(2\right)=0.5\cdot 2^{3} - 6\cdot 2^{2} + 18\cdot 2 + 40$$

$$D\left(2\right)=56$$

The value is $56$ thousand litres per hour, exactly the figure in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Evaluating a polynomial is substitution and nothing more: put the number in place of every occurrence of the variable and finish the arithmetic.

$$D(t)=0.5t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 18t + 40$$

Substituting $t=4$ term by term:

$$D\left(4\right)=0.5\cdot 4^{3} - 6\cdot 4^{2} + 18\cdot 4 + 40$$

$$D\left(4\right)=48$$

The value is $48$ thousand litres per hour while the claim reports $52$ thousand litres per hour, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

An average rate of change is the total change in the output divided by the change in the input, so both endpoint values are needed first.

$$D(t)=0.5t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 18t + 40$$

$$D\left(0\right)=40\qquad D\left(4\right)=48$$

Dividing the change in the output by the change in the input:

$$\frac{48-\left(40\right)}{4-\left(0\right)}=2$$

The average rate is $2$ thousand litres per hour, per hour, which is what the claim asks for, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Noon is six hours after 6 a.m., so the two readings to compare are $D(6)$ and $D(0)$.

$$D(t)=0.5t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 18t + 40$$

$$D\left(6\right)=0.5\cdot 6^{3} - 6\cdot 6^{2} + 18\cdot 6 + 40=40$$

$$D\left(0\right)=40$$

Both moments give $40$ thousand litres per hour, so the model has returned to its starting level, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Whether a modelled quantity rises or falls at a given moment is settled by the sign of its rate of change, which is the derivative of the model.

$$D(t)=0.5t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 18t + 40$$

$$D'(t)=1.5t^{2} - 12t + 18$$

Substituting $t=4$:

$$D'\left(4\right)=1.5\cdot 4^{2} - 12\cdot 4 + 18=-6$$

The rate is $-6\ \text{thousand litres per hour}^{2}$, which is negative, so $D$ is actually falling there, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The model is a cubic in the hours since 6 a.m.

$$D(t)=0.5t^{3} - 6t^{2} + 18t + 40$$

$$D(0)=40\qquad D(2)=56\qquad D(4)=48\qquad D(6)=40$$

The draw climbs to a morning peak, sags back through the middle of the day and returns to its 6 a.m. level at noon. Its rate of change is

$$D'(t)=1.5t^{2} - 12t + 18$$

which is negative at $t=4$, so the quantity is falling there even though the average across the first four hours is positive.

tasks.title: Reading a Degree Off a Difference Table
tasks.context: A laboratory records one measurement at each of the settings $n=0,1,2,3,4,5$, which are equally spaced. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Differencing the measurements three times gives a constant row.
Differencing the measurements twice already gives a constant row.
A polynomial of degree $3$ in $n$ reproduces every entry of the table.
Continuing the pattern, the measurement at $n=6$ would be $228$.
The measurements grow by the same amount from one setting to the next.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

For inputs spaced equally apart, differencing a table repeatedly strips one degree away each time, so a polynomial of degree $k$ flattens out to a constant exactly at the $k$-th round of differences.

$$\text{first differences}: 3,\ 9,\ 21,\ 39,\ 63$$

$$\text{second differences}: 6,\ 12,\ 18,\ 24$$

$$\text{third differences}: 6,\ 6,\ 6$$

The third row repeats the single value $6$ all the way across.

The third differences of the recorded measurements are constant, which is what the claim describes, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

For inputs spaced equally apart, differencing a table repeatedly strips one degree away each time, so a polynomial of degree $k$ flattens out to a constant exactly at the $k$-th round of differences.

$$\text{first differences}: 3,\ 9,\ 21,\ 39,\ 63$$

$$\text{second differences}: 6,\ 12,\ 18,\ 24$$

The second row still moves, so the flattening has not happened yet.

The second differences of the recorded measurements are not constant, contrary to the claim, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

Each round of differencing removes one degree, so the round at which the row first goes flat names the degree of the polynomial behind equally spaced data.

$$\text{first differences}: 3,\ 9,\ 21,\ 39,\ 63$$

$$\text{second differences}: 6,\ 12,\ 18,\ 24$$

$$\text{third differences}: 6,\ 6,\ 6$$

The flat row appears on the third round, and a cubic through the six points is exactly what that signals.

$$f(n)=n^{3}+2n$$

That cubic reproduces $0,3,12,33,72,135$ entry for entry, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

Extending a difference table means adding one more entry to the constant row and then working back up, each row rebuilding the one above it.

$$\text{third differences}: 6,\ 6,\ 6,\ \mathbf{6}$$

$$\text{second differences}: 6,\ 12,\ 18,\ 24,\ \mathbf{30}$$

$$\text{first differences}: 3,\ 9,\ 21,\ 39,\ 63,\ \mathbf{93}$$

$$135+93=228$$

The next measurement would read $228$, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Equal steps from one entry to the next would mean the first differences never change, so the first row of the table settles the matter on its own.

$$\text{first differences}: 3,\ 9,\ 21,\ 39,\ 63$$

Those gaps grow steadily instead of repeating a single value.

The steps are all different, from $3$ up to $63$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The settings are equally spaced, so differencing is the natural tool.

$$\text{measurements}: 0,\ 3,\ 12,\ 33,\ 72,\ 135$$

$$\text{first differences}: 3,\ 9,\ 21,\ 39,\ 63$$

$$\text{second differences}: 6,\ 12,\ 18,\ 24$$

$$\text{third differences}: 6,\ 6,\ 6$$

The row goes flat on the third round, which names degree $3$; the cubic behind the data is $f(n)=n^{3}+2n$, and extending the table upwards predicts $228$ at $n=6$.

tasks.title: Quadratic or Cubic? A Revenue Table Decides
tasks.context: A subscription service records monthly revenue, in thousands of euros, for its first six months. The month numbers are equally spaced. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Differencing the revenues twice gives a constant row.
The revenue grows by the same amount every month.
A quadratic in $n$ fits the six revenue figures exactly.
Differencing the revenues three times gives a row of zeros.
Extending the pattern, month $6$ would bring in $102$ thousand euros.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

For inputs spaced equally apart, differencing a table repeatedly strips one degree away each time, so a polynomial of degree $k$ flattens out to a constant exactly at the $k$-th round of differences.

$$\text{first differences}: 2,\ 8,\ 14,\ 20,\ 26$$

$$\text{second differences}: 6,\ 6,\ 6,\ 6$$

The second row repeats the single value $6$ all the way across.

The second differences of the monthly revenues are constant, which is what the claim describes, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

For inputs spaced equally apart, differencing a table repeatedly strips one degree away each time, so a polynomial of degree $k$ flattens out to a constant exactly at the $k$-th round of differences.

$$\text{first differences}: 2,\ 8,\ 14,\ 20,\ 26$$

The first row still moves, so the flattening has not happened yet.

The first differences of the monthly revenues are not constant, contrary to the claim, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The row that first becomes constant names the degree, because each round of differencing peels one degree away.

$$\text{first differences}: 2,\ 8,\ 14,\ 20,\ 26$$

$$\text{second differences}: 6,\ 6,\ 6,\ 6$$

The second round is already flat, so a polynomial of degree $2$ is enough; fitting one to the first three points gives

$$R(n)=3n^{2}-n+2$$

That quadratic returns $2,4,12,26,46,72$ in order, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

For inputs spaced equally apart, differencing a table repeatedly strips one degree away each time, so a polynomial of degree $k$ flattens out to a constant exactly at the $k$-th round of differences.

$$\text{first differences}: 2,\ 8,\ 14,\ 20,\ 26$$

$$\text{second differences}: 6,\ 6,\ 6,\ 6$$

$$\text{third differences}: 0,\ 0,\ 0$$

The third row repeats the single value $0$ all the way across.

The third differences of the monthly revenues are constant, which is what the claim describes, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Extending the table means repeating the constant row once more and then rebuilding the rows above it.

$$\text{second differences}: 6,\ 6,\ 6,\ 6,\ \mathbf{6}$$

$$\text{first differences}: 2,\ 8,\ 14,\ 20,\ 26,\ \mathbf{32}$$

$$72+32=104$$

The fitted quadratic agrees:

$$R(6)=3\cdot 36-6+2=104$$

Month $6$ would bring $104$ thousand euros, not $102$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Six equally spaced readings invite a difference table.

$$\text{revenues}: 2,\ 4,\ 12,\ 26,\ 46,\ 72$$

$$\text{first differences}: 2,\ 8,\ 14,\ 20,\ 26$$

$$\text{second differences}: 6,\ 6,\ 6,\ 6$$

Flat on the second round means degree $2$, so the third differences are all zero and the fitted model is

$$R(n)=3n^{2}-n+2$$

which predicts $104$ for month $6$.

tasks.title: Zeros, Factors and How Many There Can Be
tasks.context: Let $P$ be a polynomial function with real coefficients and let $c$ be a real number. No formula and no numerical data are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $P(c)=0$, then $\left(x-c\right)$ is a factor of $P(x)$.
If $\left(x-c\right)$ is a factor of $P(x)$, then $P(c)=0$.
A polynomial of degree $n\ge 1$ can have more than $n$ distinct real zeros.
Every polynomial of degree $3$ has at least one real zero.
Every polynomial of degree $4$ has at least one real zero.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Dividing $P$ by a linear bracket leaves a quotient and a constant remainder, because the remainder has to be of lower degree than the divisor.

$$P(x)=\left(x-c\right)Q(x)+r$$

Substituting $x=c$ closes the bracket and exposes the remainder on its own.

$$P(c)=0\cdot Q(c)+r=r$$

So the remainder is the value $P(c)$, and here that value is $0$.

$$P(x)=\left(x-c\right)Q(x)$$

With no remainder left, the bracket is a genuine factor, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Being a factor means the polynomial can be written as that bracket times something else, with nothing left over.

$$P(x)=\left(x-c\right)Q(x)$$

Substituting $x=c$ makes the first factor vanish, and a product with a zero factor is zero whatever the other factor happens to be.

$$P(c)=0\cdot Q(c)=0$$

The value at $c$ has to be $0$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

Every distinct zero contributes its own linear factor, and those factors multiply together inside the polynomial.

$$P(x)=\left(x-c_{1}\right)\left(x-c_{2}\right)\cdots\left(x-c_{k}\right)Q(x)$$

Each bracket raises the degree by one, so $k$ distinct zeros already demand degree at least $k$.

$$k\le n$$

More than $n$ distinct zeros would force a degree above $n$, which contradicts the assumption, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

For an odd degree the two arms of the graph are governed by the same leading term but by opposite signs of $x^{3}$, so they leave in opposite directions.

$$P(x)=a x^{3}+\left(\text{lower powers}\right)$$

One arm therefore ends up above the horizontal axis and the other below it, and a polynomial graph has no jumps or breaks anywhere.

$$P(x_{1})<0<P(x_{2})$$

An unbroken curve running from below the axis to above it has to meet it somewhere, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

An even degree sends both arms of the graph the same way, so nothing forces the curve to reach the horizontal axis at all.

$$P(x)=x^{4}+1$$

A fourth power is never negative, so the smallest value this polynomial can take is at $x=0$.

$$P(x)\ge 1>0$$

This degree-$4$ polynomial stays strictly above the axis and so has no real zero, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Two structural facts carry all five claims. First, division by a linear bracket leaves a constant remainder equal to the value there, which ties zeros and factors together.

$$P(x)=\left(x-c\right)Q(x)+P(c)$$

Second, each distinct zero costs one degree, so a degree-$n$ polynomial cannot have more than $n$ of them. Parity then decides existence: an odd degree forces the arms apart and guarantees a crossing, while an even degree does not.

$$x^{4}+1\ge 1>0$$

tasks.title: A Repeated Bracket Inside a Quartic
tasks.context: A quartic function factorises as $P(x)=\left(x-2\right)^{2}\left(x+1\right)\left(x-3\right)$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $P$ has exactly three distinct real zeros.
The degree of $P$ is $4$.
At $x=2$ the graph of $P$ touches the horizontal axis without crossing it.
The graph of $P$ crosses the horizontal axis four times.
The graph of $P$ crosses the vertical axis at $\left(0,12\right)$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Zeros come from the brackets, but a bracket that appears twice still names only one number, so the count of distinct zeros can fall short of the degree.

$$P(x)=x^{4} - 6x^{3} + 9x^{2} + 4x - 12$$

$$P\left(x\right)=\left(x+1\right)\left(x-2\right)\left(x-3\right)$$

Each bracket contributes the number that makes it vanish: $x=-1$, $x=2$, $x=3$.

There are three distinct real zeros, exactly the count claimed, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The degree is the largest power of the variable that still carries a non-zero coefficient, so order the terms by falling powers and look at the first one.

$$P(x)=x^{4} - 6x^{3} + 9x^{2} + 4x - 12$$

The largest power present is $x^{4}$, and its coefficient $1$ is not zero.

$$\text{degree of }P=4$$

The degree is $4$, exactly the number in the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Crossing requires the values on the two sides of a zero to have opposite signs, so the shape at a zero is decided by how many times its bracket appears.

$$P(x)=\left(x-2\right)^{2}\left(x+1\right)\left(x-3\right)$$

The bracket $\left(x-2\right)^{2}$ is a square and never turns negative, so the sign near $x=2$ is set by the remaining two brackets, which are both close to $3$ and $-1$ there.

$$P(1.9)=-0.0319\qquad P(2.1)=-0.0279$$

Both neighbours sit below the axis, so the curve comes up to the axis and turns back down, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A quartic has at most four zeros counted with repeats, but repeats do not produce extra meetings with the axis and a squared bracket does not even produce a crossing.

$$P(x)=\left(x-2\right)^{2}\left(x+1\right)\left(x-3\right)$$

The brackets vanish at $x=-1$, $x=2$ and $x=3$ only, and of those the middle one is a touch rather than a crossing.

$$\text{crossings}=2\qquad \text{touches}=1$$

The curve genuinely passes through the axis twice, at $x=-1$ and $x=3$, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The graph meets the vertical axis where the input is $0$, and at that input every term with a power of the variable disappears — only the constant term survives.

$$P(x)=x^{4} - 6x^{3} + 9x^{2} + 4x - 12$$

$$P\left(0\right)=-12$$

The crossing sits at height $-12$, not at $12$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Multiplying the brackets out gives the expanded quartic,

$$P(x)=x^{4} - 6x^{3} + 9x^{2} + 4x - 12$$

but the factored form is the useful one:

$$P(x)=\left(x-2\right)^{2}\left(x+1\right)\left(x-3\right)$$

There are three distinct zeros, $-1$, $2$ and $3$. The squared bracket makes $x=2$ a touching point, while the two single brackets are genuine crossings.

$$P(0)=-12$$

tasks.title: Matching a Picture to a Product of Brackets
tasks.context: The figure shows the graph of a cubic function $f$ on the window $-2\le x\le 3.5$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The curve shown is the graph of $y=\left(x+1\right)\left(x-2\right)^{2}$.
The curve shown is the graph of $y=\left(x+1\right)^{2}\left(x-2\right)$.
The graph of $f$ crosses the vertical axis at $\left(0,4\right)$.
The graph of $f$ has exactly two turning points.
At $x=3$ the graph of $f$ lies below the horizontal axis.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Two polynomials describe the same curve only when they expand to the very same coefficients, so multiply the offered product out and compare.

$$y=\left(x+1\right)\left(x-2\right)^{2}$$

$$\left(x+1\right)\left(x-2\right)^{2}=x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 4$$

The function behind the picture is

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 4$$

The two expansions agree coefficient for coefficient, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Two polynomials describe the same curve only when they expand to the very same coefficients, so multiply the offered product out and compare.

$$y=\left(x+1\right)^{2}\left(x-2\right)$$

$$\left(x+1\right)^{2}\left(x-2\right)=x^{3} - 3x - 2$$

The function behind the picture is

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 4$$

The two expansions differ by $-3x^{2} + 3x + 6$, which is not the zero polynomial, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The graph meets the vertical axis where the input is $0$, and at that input every term with a power of the variable disappears — only the constant term survives.

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 4$$

$$f\left(0\right)=4$$

The crossing sits at height $4$, exactly where the claim puts it, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

A turning point is a place where the curve stops rising and starts falling, or the other way round; a polynomial of degree $n$ can have at most $n-1$ of them.

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 4$$

The picture changes direction at $x\approx 0$, $x\approx 2$, and between those places the curve keeps one direction throughout.

$$\text{turning points of }f=2$$

There are two turning points, the number the claim names, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Whether the curve runs under or over the horizontal axis at a given input is decided by the sign of the value there, so evaluate and look at the sign.

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 4$$

$$f\left(3\right)=3^{3} - 3\cdot 3^{2} + 4=4$$

The value $4$ is positive, so the curve runs above the axis there, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The drawing shows a cubic that crosses the axis once on the left and then comes down to touch it before climbing away, which is the signature of one single bracket and one squared bracket.

$$f(x)=\left(x+1\right)\left(x-2\right)^{2}$$

$$f(x)=x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 4$$

The crossing is at $x=-1$ and the touch is at $x=2$; the vertical axis is met at height $4$, which is also the local maximum of the curve.

$$f(0)=4\qquad f(2)=0\qquad f(3)=4$$

Swapping which bracket is squared would move both features and give a different cubic altogether.

tasks.title: A Quartic Turned Upside Down
tasks.context: The figure shows the graph of a polynomial function $g$ on the window $-2.6\le x\le 2.6$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: As $x$ grows beyond every bound, $g\left(x\right)$ falls below every bound.
The curve meets the horizontal axis exactly four times.
The graph of $g$ crosses the vertical axis at $\left(0,-4\right)$.
The graph of $g$ has exactly two turning points.
The largest value $g$ takes on the window is reached at $x=0$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Far away from the origin the highest power dwarfs everything else, so the far ends of the graph are decided by the leading term alone.

$$g(x)=-x^{4} + 5x^{2} - 4$$

$$\text{leading term}=-x^{4}$$

The exponent $4$ is even and the coefficient $-1$ is negative, which fixes both ends of the picture.

On that side the values fall below every bound, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

The crossings are the zeros, and the expression comes apart into four linear brackets once the minus sign is pulled out front.

$$g(x)=-x^{4} + 5x^{2} - 4$$

$$g\left(x\right)=\left(-1\right)\left(x+2\right)\left(x+1\right)\left(x-1\right)\left(x-2\right)$$

Each bracket contributes the number that makes it vanish: $x=-2$, $x=-1$, $x=1$, $x=2$.

There are four distinct real zeros, exactly the count claimed, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

The graph meets the vertical axis where the input is $0$, and at that input every term with a power of the variable disappears — only the constant term survives.

$$g(x)=-x^{4} + 5x^{2} - 4$$

$$g\left(0\right)=-4$$

The crossing sits at height $-4$, exactly where the claim puts it, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

A turning point is a place where the curve stops rising and starts falling, or the other way round; a polynomial of degree $n$ can have at most $n-1$ of them.

$$g(x)=-x^{4} + 5x^{2} - 4$$

The picture changes direction at $x\approx -1.58$, $x\approx 0$, $x\approx 1.58$, and between those places the curve keeps one direction throughout.

$$\text{turning points of }g=3$$

There are three turning points while the claim insists on two, so the statement is False.

**E.** → False

The value at $x=0$ is only the constant term, and the picture shows two humps rising above it on either side, so the peak must be looked for away from the vertical axis.

$$g(x)=-x^{4} + 5x^{2} - 4$$

$$g(0)=-4$$

The humps sit where the curve turns, at $x=\pm\sqrt{\frac{5}{2}}\approx \pm 1.58$, and there the value is

$$g\left(\pm 1.58\right)\approx 2.25$$

The value $2.25$ on the humps beats the $-4$ at the origin, so $x=0$ is a local low point rather than the highest place, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The curve in the picture belongs to

$$g(x)=-x^{4} + 5x^{2} - 4$$

$$g(x)=-\left(x+2\right)\left(x+1\right)\left(x-1\right)\left(x-2\right)$$

so it crosses the axis at $x=-2,-1,1,2$ and passes the vertical axis at $-4$. The leading coefficient is negative and the degree even, so both arms plunge.

$$g(0)=-4\qquad g\left(\pm 1.58\right)\approx 2.25$$

Between the four crossings the curve turns three times: two humps above the axis and the dip at the origin between them.

tasks.title: Marginal Cost From a Cubic Cost Function
tasks.context: A plant's total weekly cost in euros is modelled by $C(q)=0.02q^{3} - 1.5q^{2} + 40q + 500$, where $q$ is the number of units produced and $0\le q\le 60$. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: $C\left(10\right)=770$ euros.
The marginal cost function of the plant is $C'(q)=0.06q^{2} - 3q + 40$.
Marginal cost is at its lowest at an output of $20$ units.
At an output of $10$ units the total cost is still rising.
Raising output from $0$ to $20$ units costs on average $25$ euros per extra unit.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Evaluating a polynomial is substitution and nothing more: put the number in place of every occurrence of the variable and finish the arithmetic.

$$C(q)=0.02q^{3} - 1.5q^{2} + 40q + 500$$

Substituting $q=10$ term by term:

$$C\left(10\right)=0.02\cdot 10^{3} - 1.5\cdot 10^{2} + 40\cdot 10 + 500$$

$$C\left(10\right)=770$$

The value is $770$ euros, exactly the figure in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Marginal cost is the rate at which total cost changes with output, so it is the derivative of the cost model, taken term by term.

$$C(q)=0.02q^{3} - 1.5q^{2} + 40q + 500$$

Each power drops by one and picks up its old exponent as a factor, while the fixed cost $500$ contributes nothing to the rate.

$$C'(q)=0.06q^{2} - 3q + 40$$

That is exactly the expression written in the claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The marginal cost is a quadratic in $q$ with a positive leading coefficient, so it opens upwards and takes its lowest value on its axis of symmetry.

$$C'(q)=0.06q^{2} - 3q + 40$$

$$q=-\frac{b}{2a}=\frac{3}{2\cdot 0.06}=25$$

At that output the marginal cost is

$$C'\left(25\right)=0.06\cdot 25^{2} - 3\cdot 25 + 40=2.5$$

The cheapest extra unit comes at $q=25$, not at $q=20$, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

Total cost rises exactly where marginal cost is positive, so the sign of the derivative at that output settles the claim.

$$C(q)=0.02q^{3} - 1.5q^{2} + 40q + 500$$

$$C'(q)=0.06q^{2} - 3q + 40$$

Substituting $q=10$:

$$C'\left(10\right)=0.06\cdot 10^{2} - 3\cdot 10 + 40=16$$

The rate is $16\ \text{euros per unit}$, which is positive, so $C$ is rising there, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

An average rate of change is the total change in the output divided by the change in the input, so both endpoint values are needed first.

$$C(q)=0.02q^{3} - 1.5q^{2} + 40q + 500$$

$$C\left(0\right)=500\qquad C\left(20\right)=860$$

Dividing the change in the output by the change in the input:

$$\frac{860-\left(500\right)}{20-\left(0\right)}=18$$

The average rate is $18$ euros per unit, which fails the comparison in the claim, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
The cost model is a cubic in output, and its derivative is the marginal cost.

$$C(q)=0.02q^{3} - 1.5q^{2} + 40q + 500$$

$$C'(q)=0.06q^{2} - 3q + 40$$

Marginal cost is a quadratic opening upwards, so it dips to a minimum on its axis of symmetry at $q=25$ and is positive well before that, which is why total cost keeps climbing.

$$C'(10)=16\qquad C'(25)=2.5$$

Total cost itself moves from $500$ at zero output to $860$ at twenty units.

$$\frac{C(20)-C(0)}{20-0}=\frac{360}{20}=18$$

tasks.title: Two-Hourly Output From a Wind Farm Log
tasks.context: A wind farm's control room records the total energy delivered since midnight, in megawatt hours, at the end of every second hour. No formula is fitted to the readings; the bar chart shows the average output on each two-hour stretch, in megawatt hours per hour. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Across the whole twenty hours the farm averaged $5.25$ MWh per hour.
The best two-hour stretch of the day was from hour $6$ to hour $8$.
Exactly two of the interior stretches deliver more than both of their neighbours.
Hours $8$ to $10$ delivered less energy than hours $6$ to $8$.
The running totals grow along a straight line, so a polynomial of degree $1$ reproduces the log exactly.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

An average output is the total energy divided by the total time, so only the first and last readings of the log are needed.

$$\bar P=\frac{105-0}{20-0}$$

$$\bar P=5.25\ \text{MWh per hour}$$

The overall average is $5.25$ MWh per hour, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

Every stretch lasts the same two hours, so the best stretch is simply the one on which the running total gained the most.

$$\bar P_{6\text{–}8}=\frac{38-24}{2}=7\ \text{MWh per hour}$$

The largest gain in the log is the jump from $47$ to $62$ megawatt hours:

$$\bar P_{10\text{–}12}=\frac{62-47}{2}=\frac{15}{2}\ \text{MWh per hour}$$

The record belongs to hours $10$ to $12$ at $\frac{15}{2}$ MWh per hour, so the statement is False.

**C.** → False

A stretch beats both neighbours whenever the sequence of stretch averages rises into it and falls out of it again, so read the bars in order.

$$3,\ 5,\ 4,\ 7,\ \frac{9}{2},\ \frac{15}{2},\ \frac{11}{2},\ \frac{7}{2},\ \frac{13}{2},\ 6$$

The bars turn downwards immediately after the values $5$,\ $7$,\ $\frac{15}{2}$,\ $\frac{13}{2}$, each of which is taller than both of its neighbours.

There are four such stretches rather than two, so the statement is False.

**D.** → True

The energy delivered on a stretch is the gain in the running total across it, so subtract consecutive readings.

$$47-38=9\ \text{MWh}$$

$$38-24=14\ \text{MWh}$$

The later stretch delivered $9$ megawatt hours against $14$ for the earlier one, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Straight-line growth means the running total gains the same amount every stretch, which is exactly the statement that the first differences never change.

$$\text{gains}: 6,\ 10,\ 8,\ 14,\ 9,\ 15,\ 11,\ 7,\ 13,\ 12$$
