Those gains jump around instead of repeating a single value, and the bar chart shows the same restlessness.

No linear model can match a log whose gains range from $6$ up to $15$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
There is no formula here, only a log, so every rate is a gain divided by the two hours in which it happened.

$$\bar P_{i}=\frac{E_{i+1}-E_{i}}{2}$$

The ten stretch averages, in megawatt hours per hour, are

$$3,\ 5,\ 4,\ 7,\ \frac{9}{2},\ \frac{15}{2},\ \frac{11}{2},\ \frac{7}{2},\ \frac{13}{2},\ 6$$

The record stretch is hours $10$ to $12$ at $7.5$, four separate stretches beat both of their neighbours, and the whole day averages

$$\frac{105}{20}=5.25\ \text{MWh per hour}$$

Because those gains keep changing, the running total is nowhere near a straight line.

tasks.title: Testing a Proposed Cubic Against a Table
tasks.context: An analyst logs the cumulative number of installations after each of the first five weeks and proposes the model $f(n)=n^{3} - 2n^{2} + 5n$, where $n$ is the week number. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: The proposed model reproduces the week-$3$ entry of the table.
Differencing the recorded totals three times gives a constant row.
Differencing the recorded totals twice already gives a constant row.
The model predicts $172$ installations in total by the end of week $6$.
The week-$4$ total is larger than the week-$1$ and week-$2$ totals added together.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Testing a model against a table is substitution: put the week number in and see whether the recorded figure comes back out.

$$f(n)=n^{3} - 2n^{2} + 5n$$

Substituting $n=3$ term by term:

$$f\left(3\right)=3^{3} - 2\cdot 3^{2} + 5\cdot 3$$

$$f\left(3\right)=24$$

The value is $24$ installations, exactly the figure in the claim, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

For inputs spaced equally apart, differencing a table repeatedly strips one degree away each time, so a polynomial of degree $k$ flattens out to a constant exactly at the $k$-th round of differences.

$$\text{first differences}: 6,\ 14,\ 28,\ 48$$

$$\text{second differences}: 8,\ 14,\ 20$$

$$\text{third differences}: 6,\ 6$$

The third row repeats the single value $6$ all the way across.

The third differences of the cumulative installations are constant, which is what the claim describes, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

For inputs spaced equally apart, differencing a table repeatedly strips one degree away each time, so a polynomial of degree $k$ flattens out to a constant exactly at the $k$-th round of differences.

$$\text{first differences}: 6,\ 14,\ 28,\ 48$$

$$\text{second differences}: 8,\ 14,\ 20$$

The second row still moves, so the flattening has not happened yet.

The second differences of the cumulative installations are not constant, contrary to the claim, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

Evaluating a polynomial is substitution and nothing more: put the number in place of every occurrence of the variable and finish the arithmetic.

$$f(n)=n^{3} - 2n^{2} + 5n$$

Substituting $n=6$ term by term:

$$f\left(6\right)=6^{3} - 2\cdot 6^{2} + 5\cdot 6$$

$$f\left(6\right)=174$$

The value is $174$ installations while the claim reports $172$ installations, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

This is a comparison of recorded figures, so no model is needed at all — just the rows themselves.

$$4+10=14$$

$$52>14$$

The week-$4$ total of $52$ comfortably clears the combined $14$ of the first two weeks, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
The proposed model is a cubic in the week number.

$$f(n)=n^{3} - 2n^{2} + 5n$$

$$f(1)=4\qquad f(2)=10\qquad f(3)=24\qquad f(4)=52\qquad f(5)=100$$

Those are precisely the recorded totals, so the model fits, and its own difference table confirms the degree:

$$\text{first differences}: 6,\ 14,\ 28,\ 48$$

$$\text{second differences}: 8,\ 14,\ 20$$

$$\text{third differences}: 6,\ 6$$

Extending the model one week further gives

$$f(6)=216-72+30=174$$

tasks.title: Symmetry, Parity and the Shape of the Arms
tasks.context: Let $P$ be a polynomial function with real coefficients. Nothing is said about its coefficients beyond what each statement assumes. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If every power appearing in $P(x)$ is even, then the graph of $P$ is symmetric about the horizontal axis.
If every power appearing in $P(x)$ is odd, then $P(-x)=-P(x)$ holds for every real $x$.
A polynomial in which only odd powers appear must pass through the origin.
If $P$ has odd degree, then the number of its distinct real zeros is odd.
If $P$ has even degree, then the two arms of its graph head in the same direction.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → False

Symmetry about the horizontal axis would mean that whenever a height belongs to the graph, so does its negative — and that cannot happen for a function, which allots one height to each input.

$$P(-x)=P(x)$$

Even powers do give a symmetry, but the mirror is the vertical axis: replacing $x$ by $-x$ leaves each even power alone.

$$\left(-x\right)^{2}=x^{2}\qquad \left(-x\right)^{4}=x^{4}$$

The mirror line is the vertical axis, not the horizontal one, so the statement is False.

**B.** → True

An odd power carries a change of sign in its input straight through to the output, because the minus sign is used an odd number of times.

$$\left(-x\right)^{3}=-x^{3}\qquad \left(-x\right)^{5}=-x^{5}$$

Every term of $P$ therefore flips sign at once, and a common factor of $-1$ can be taken outside the whole sum.

$$P(-x)=-\left(a_{1}x+a_{3}x^{3}+\cdots\right)=-P(x)$$

The identity holds for every real $x$, so the statement is True.

**C.** → True

Passing through the origin means the value at $x=0$ is $0$, so only the constant term of the polynomial matters.

$$P(x)=a_{1}x+a_{3}x^{3}+a_{5}x^{5}+\cdots$$

A constant term would be $a_{0}x^{0}$, an even power, so it is absent by assumption and every remaining term dies at $x=0$.

$$P(0)=0$$

The graph is forced through $(0,0)$, so the statement is True.

**D.** → False

An odd degree does guarantee at least one crossing, because the two arms of the graph head in opposite directions, but it says nothing about how the zeros in between are arranged.

$$P(x)=x^{2}\left(x-1\right)$$

This cubic has odd degree, yet its distinct zeros are only $x=0$ and $x=1$, because the bracket at $0$ is repeated.

$$\text{distinct real zeros}=2$$

Two is an even count, so the rule fails already here, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

For inputs far from the origin the leading term dwarfs the rest, so both arms are governed by $a x^{n}$ alone.

$$P(x)\approx a x^{n}\quad\text{for large }\left|x\right|$$

With $n$ even, the power $x^{n}$ is positive on both sides, so the sign of $a$ decides one common direction for both arms.

$$\left(-x\right)^{n}=x^{n}\quad\text{for even }n$$

Both arms rise when $a>0$ and both fall when $a<0$, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Two ideas run through all five claims. Replacing $x$ by $-x$ leaves even powers untouched and flips odd ones, which is where the symmetries come from.

$$\left(-x\right)^{n}=x^{n}\ (n\text{ even})\qquad \left(-x\right)^{n}=-x^{n}\ (n\text{ odd})$$

And far from the origin the leading term decides both arms, so an even degree sends them the same way while an odd degree splits them. Counting distinct zeros, however, is a separate matter: repeated brackets shorten the list.

$$x^{2}\left(x-1\right)\ \text{has degree }3\ \text{but two zeros}$$

tasks.title: What Division Leaves Behind
tasks.context: Let $P$ and $Q$ be polynomial functions with real coefficients, and consider dividing one by the other. No coefficients are supplied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: If $P$ has degree $5$ and is divided by a polynomial of degree $2$, the quotient has degree $3$.
In that division the remainder has degree at most $2$.
If $P(1)=0$ and $P(2)=0$, then $\left(x-1\right)\left(x-2\right)$ divides $P(x)$.
If $P(3)=5$, then $\left(x-3\right)$ is a factor of $P(x)-5$.
If $P$ and $Q$ both have degree $4$, then $P-Q$ has degree $4$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

Division writes the dividend as divisor times quotient plus a remainder of lower degree than the divisor, and degrees add across that product.

$$P(x)=Q(x)S(x)+R(x)$$

The remainder cannot reach degree $5$, since its degree is below $2$, so the leading term of $P$ has to come from the product.

$$5=2+\text{degree of }S$$

The quotient is forced to have degree $3$, so the statement is True.

**B.** → False

The whole point of stopping the division is that the remainder can no longer be divided by the divisor, which means its degree has dropped below the divisor's.

$$\text{degree of }R<\text{degree of }Q=2$$

A remainder of degree $2$ could still be divided once more, so the process would not have finished.

$$\text{degree of }R\le 1$$

The genuine ceiling is $1$, one below the divisor's degree, so the statement is False.

**C.** → True

The first zero hands over a factor straight away, by the same argument that turns any zero into a bracket.

$$P(x)=\left(x-1\right)S(x)$$

Substituting $x=2$ into that identity uses the second zero; the first bracket becomes $1$, so the burden falls on $S$.

$$0=P(2)=\left(2-1\right)S(2)=S(2)$$

So $S$ itself has a zero at $2$ and therefore carries the second bracket.

$$P(x)=\left(x-1\right)\left(x-2\right)T(x)$$

The product of the two brackets divides $P$ exactly, so the statement is True.

**D.** → True

A bracket is a factor of a polynomial exactly when the polynomial vanishes at the matching number, so look at the shifted function rather than at $P$ itself.

$$H(x)=P(x)-5$$

Evaluating $H$ at $3$ uses the one piece of information given.

$$H(3)=P(3)-5=5-5=0$$

The shifted polynomial has a zero at $3$, so the bracket divides it, so the statement is True.

**E.** → False

Subtracting collects matching powers, and when two polynomials share the same degree their leading terms can annihilate each other.

$$P(x)=x^{4}+x\qquad Q(x)=x^{4}-1$$

Both have degree $4$, but the quartic terms cancel exactly and what survives is far smaller.

$$P(x)-Q(x)=x+1$$

The difference here has degree $1$, not $4$, so the statement is False.
tasks.solution_overview:
Division of polynomials always takes the same shape, with a remainder strictly below the divisor in degree.

$$P(x)=Q(x)S(x)+R(x),\qquad \text{degree of }R<\text{degree of }Q$$

Degrees add across the product, which pins the quotient down. Zeros and brackets are interchangeable, and the trick extends to shifted functions such as $P(x)-5$. Only subtraction breaks the pattern: equal degrees may cancel.

$$\left(x^{4}+x\right)-\left(x^{4}-1\right)=x+1$$

tasks.title: The Family $x^{3}-ax$ as the Parameter Moves
tasks.context: For each real number $a>0$ define the polynomial function $P_{a}(x)=x^{3}-ax$. Statements below must hold for the whole family unless a particular $a$ is named. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Every member of the family passes through the origin.
Every member of the family has three distinct real zeros.
Every member of the family has exactly three turning points.
There is a value $a>0$ for which the graph of $P_{a}$ has no turning point at all.
For $a=12$ the local maximum of $P_{a}$ sits at $x=-2$.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** → True

A curve runs through the origin when the value at $x=0$ is $0$, and at that input every term carrying a power of $x$ disappears.

$$P_{a}(x)=x^{3}-ax$$

There is no constant term to survive, whatever the parameter happens to be.

$$P_{a}(0)=0$$

The origin lies on every curve of the family, so the statement is True.

**B.** → True

Pulling the common factor $x$ out reduces the hunt for zeros to a factor of $x$ and a difference of squares.

$$P_{a}(x)=x\left(x^{2}-a\right)$$

Because $a$ is strictly positive it has a real square root, and the second bracket then splits as well.

$$P_{a}(x)=x\left(x-\sqrt{a}\right)\left(x+\sqrt{a}\right)$$

The three numbers $0$, $\sqrt{a}$ and $-\sqrt{a}$ are different from one another precisely because $\sqrt{a}>0$.

Every member has three distinct real zeros, so the statement is True.

**C.** → False

The curve turns where its rate of change vanishes, so differentiate the family once and count the solutions.

$$P_{a}'(x)=3x^{2}-a$$

That is a quadratic, and a quadratic cannot vanish at more than two places.

$$x=\pm\sqrt{\frac{a}{3}}$$

Each member turns exactly twice, and a cubic can never manage three turns, so the statement is False.

**D.** → False

A turning point needs the rate of change to vanish, so ask when the derivative has no real solution.

$$P_{a}'(x)=3x^{2}-a=0$$

$$x^{2}=\frac{a}{3}$$

With $a>0$ the right-hand side is strictly positive, so it always has two real square roots — the equation can never come out empty.

Every positive parameter delivers two turning points, so no such $a$ exists, so the statement is False.

**E.** → True

The turning points come from the derivative, and with a positive leading coefficient the left-hand one is the local maximum: the curve climbs into it and falls away after it.

$$P_{12}'(x)=3x^{2}-12$$

$$3x^{2}=12\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=\pm 2$$

The left turning point is at $x=-2$, and the height there is

$$P_{12}(-2)=\left(-2\right)^{3}-12\left(-2\right)=16$$

The local maximum of this member is the point $\left(-2,16\right)$, so the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
Factoring the family once answers most of the questions.

$$P_{a}(x)=x\left(x-\sqrt{a}\right)\left(x+\sqrt{a}\right)$$

For every $a>0$ there are three distinct zeros, and the origin is always one of them. Differentiating gives a quadratic, so there are always exactly two turning points and never more, never fewer.

$$P_{a}'(x)=3x^{2}-a\qquad x=\pm\sqrt{\frac{a}{3}}$$

With $a=12$ those turning points land on $x=\pm 2$, the left one being the local maximum at height $16$.
